lesson.title: The Body's Three-Act Response to Stress: General Adaptation Syndrome
lesson.summary: Hans Selye's General Adaptation Syndrome describes the body's response to ongoing stress as unfolding in three predictable stages, alarm, resistance, and exhaustion, if a stressor continues without relief.
lesson.body:
Hans Selye, an endocrinologist, observed through laboratory research that the body tends to respond to many different kinds of stressors, physical, emotional, or otherwise, with a broadly similar, nonspecific physiological pattern. He used the term stress, in this biological sense, to describe that response, and he described how it unfolds over time as the General Adaptation Syndrome, or GAS, made up of three stages.

The first stage is alarm. This is the body's initial jolt of activation when a stressor first appears, and it maps closely onto the sympathetic nervous system activation covered in the fight-flight-freeze chapter later in this unit: stress hormones like adrenaline surge, and the body rapidly mobilizes energy for immediate action.

If the stressor does not resolve quickly, the body moves into the second stage, resistance. Here, the intense sympathetic arousal of the alarm stage settles somewhat, but stress hormones such as cortisol remain elevated as the body works to sustain heightened functioning while simultaneously trying to adapt and repair. A person may continue functioning reasonably well outwardly during resistance, even holding up under real pressure, while physiological resources are quietly and steadily being drawn down in the background.

If the stressor persists long enough without adequate relief, the body's adaptive resources become depleted, entering the third stage, exhaustion. Immune functioning can weaken during this stage, leaving a person more vulnerable to illness, alongside fatigue and burnout. The parasympathetic nervous system matters here too: a healthy stress response normally includes periods of recovery, when parasympathetic activity supports rest and restoration between stressful demands. Chronic stress that never allows this recovery window, that keeps the alarm-resistance cycle running without pause, is a major part of what pushes the system toward exhaustion.

It is worth noting some context about this model. Selye's original research was largely conducted using laboratory animals exposed to various physical stressors, studying the nonspecific pattern of bodily response those stressors produced, and the model has been refined by later stress researchers since. Even so, the three-stage alarm, resistance, exhaustion framework remains the standard, foundational way psychology describes how the body handles stress that continues over time, and it sets up the more detailed look at the alarm stage's mechanics in the next chapter, on the fight-flight-freeze response.
